title: incremental-parse-prefetch-tokens-idea-dump
content:
Overview:
This is a freeform dump of ideas and early hypotheses around incremental parsing / lightweight token prefetching for tiny requests. Goal: shave tail CPU on small requests (<= 512 bytes payload) by reducing Python-side parse/tokenize work and amortizing allocation/backpressure in worker queues. Not a polished design — sketch + experiments + short checklist so we can pick a few small quick wins.

Why this matters (context):
- We see a nontrivial fraction of our p95/p99 CPU for hosted endpoints coming from request parsing and tokenization for tiny payloads (see INF-1245).
- Python GIL and interpreter overhead amplify cost for many concurrent tiny requests — even with batching disabled.
- Existing fastpaths (C tokenizers, SIMD utf8 scanners) exist, but handoff costs, allocations, and thread wakeups dominate at small sizes.
- If we can remove ~30–50us from parse+tokenize for small requests, that directly improves tail latency and reduces required CPU capacity.

Hypotheses:
1) Incremental parsing that reads a small prefix and returns a lightweight token-count/offset map will allow us to avoid full tokenization in the hot path and defer heavy work to background workers or the model runtime when needed.
2) Prefetching the first N bytes of the request body into a preallocated buffer reduces syscalls and short-lived allocations, lowering wakeups and GC pressure.
3) A tiny C-extension FFI that performs UTF-8 boundary checks + ASCII fast-scan and returns offsets is cheaper than invoking Python tokenizers for small payloads.
4) A prioritized queue for tiny requests (dedicated worker lanes) cuts contention vs a single big threadpool.
5) Combining the above with a fast-path for short prompts that are entirely ASCII yields best ROI; non-ASCII will fall back to full tokenizer.

Design sketches / components:
A) Prefetch layer (C):
- API: prefetch_prefix(fd_or_bytes, n) -> bytes_view_or_offset + checksum
- Implementation: read(2) into preallocated arena (per-worker fast arena) up to N (configurable, e.g., 256–1024). Return a lightweight view: pointer + length. Avoid creating Python bytes when possible — expose to Python as PyMemoryView on success.
- Behavior: if request larger than N, still return prefix view and set a flag to signal full-parse later.

B) Incremental UTF-8 / token boundary scanner (C):
- Input: prefix view
- Output: array of token-boundary offsets (C array) + heuristic token count; for JSON-like inputs return index of first non-whitespace after parse; for chat-like prompts return likely token breakpoints.
- Fast-path: ASCII-only scan using memchr / vectorized load; fall back to slower code for non-ascii.
- Expose as small FFI call that returns either: (status=OK, offsets_ptr, n_offsets) or (status=FALLBACK).

C) Minimal Python-side glue:
- In request preprocessing, attempt Prefetch+IncrementalScan. If OK and token_count < threshold, synthesize a lightweight ParsedRequest object that avoids per-token Python allocs.
- Otherwise, fall back to existing tokenizer.

D) Worker lanes:
- Tiny-lane: handful (N) of threads dedicated to tiny requests; they get preallocated arenas and run the C fastpath. Larger requests go to general pool.
- Backpressure: if tiny-lane is saturated, either (a) run small request on general pool (with full parse cost), or (b) coalesce multiple tiny requests for shared parsing passes.

Experiment matrix (priority):
1) Microbench: pure C incremental scanner vs Python tokenizer (single-thread, in-process). Metric: cycle count / microsecond per 128B/256B/512B inputs (ASCII vs non-ASCII).
2) Prefetch read: compare syscall cost with small-buffer read into preallocated vs Python reading into new bytes. Metric: allocation rate, GC pause per 10k requests.
3) End-to-end p95/p99: run a small-scale replay of production tiny requests (from sampling) with feature flags on/off for C fastpath and tiny-lane. Measure latency and CPU.
4) Threadpool contention: simulate many concurrent tiny requests and measure queue length, wakeups, and context-switch counts with and without dedicated tiny lane.

Bench commands / notes:
- flamegraph: capture 30s at target RPS with perf on a dedicated instance (disable other noise).
  sudo perf record -F 200 -a -g -- sleep 30
  sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > out.svg
- python microbench harness: timeit loops with preconstructed request bytes. Use cpu-affinity to stabilize.
- allocator traces: jemalloc stats before/after 100k tiny requests to see short-lived alloc rates.

Targets / expected wins (ballpark):
- C incremental scan vs Python tokenizer: 3–6x faster for ASCII small payloads.
- Prefetch: 10–30% reduction in p50 parse time; larger benefit at p95.
- Combined with tiny-lane: 15–40% reduction in p99 for small request workload slices.

Risk and unknowns:
- Complexity: introducing C FFI + arenas increases maintenance surface and potential memory safety issues. Need careful fuzz testing.
- Coverage: many production requests contain emojis / non-ASCII; fallback paths may negate wins.
- Observability: need good tracing to know when fastpath used vs fallback.
- Interaction with network stack: prefetch + read may shift latency to kernel and coalesce syscalls in ways that complicate tail behavior.

Quick mitigation checklist:
- Start with read+memchr based incremental scanner in a separate repo / branch; keep it opt-in via feature flag.
- Add unit + fuzz tests for boundary conditions (partial multi-byte UTF-8 at end of prefix).
- Expose telemetry: fastpath_used counter, fallback_reason tag, avg_prefix_bytes.

Next steps (short-term):
- Owner: Aisha -> implement C scanner toy and run microbench (2–3 days).
- Collaborators: Luca to prototype prefetch arena in runtime; Jia to prepare replay dataset of tiny requests (anonymized).
- Set up 2 experiments in queue: microbench and small-scale p99 replay.
- Add Linear ticket INF-1245 follow-ups for implementation and rollout plan.

Notes to self / open questions:
- What threshold for "tiny" makes sense? 128B, 256B, 512B? Need to pick after distribution analysis (Jia).
- Can we reuse existing SIMD UTF-8 helpers or ship a focused minimal dependency?
- Is it worth trying to avoid Python objects entirely via a C-managed request header pool? Likely higher complexity but big wins.
- Should we consider user-level batching/cross-request prefix sharing for identical prefixes? (edge case but could be interesting).

Appendix: quick flamegraph interpretation pointers:
- Look for "PyObject_Malloc" and "unicode_" families in Python-dominated traces; if they dominate small-request tail we win by reducing Python object churn.
- If syscalls dominate (read/sendto), prefetching will not help latency much — need to check together with network traces.

End of dump. This is intentionally rough; we can pick 1 small prototype (C incremental scan + microbench) to validate whether to proceed.
